articles.title: Textures are less comfortable to view than other natural images, consistent with cortical hyper-metabolism theory
articles.content: Images considered uncomfortable to view often over-represent mid-range spatial frequencies (mid-SFs) relative to the average 1/f amplitude spectrum of natural images. A proposed mechanism for this discomfort known as the Cortical Hyper-metabolism Hypothesis (CHH) posits that such images over-activate the visual cortex, which is highly sensitive to mid-SFs. We tested a novel prediction of the CHH, namely that natural image categories like textures which over-represent mid-SFs will be less comfortable to view on average than other natural images. We indeed found that texture images were less comfortable to view than various non-textures, validating this prediction of the CHH and demonstrating its potential relevance to natural image aesthetics. Passing our images through models of early visual neurons demonstrated that the mean activity of a population of simulated log-Gabor filters resembling V1 simple cells best predicted discomfort. Manipulations which selectively altered the image phase or amplitude spectra while leaving the other intact were less comfortable than the originals, suggesting that visual comfort is not a simple function of either one of these characteristics. Our results suggest that although many factors contribute to the visual comfort of natural image categories, early visual processing may play an important role, consistent with the CHH.

articles.title: LRRC8A/D-containing anion channels mediate swelling-activated taurine release in the mouse brain
articles.content: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) are swelling-activated Cl- channels formed by heteromers of LRRC8 proteins (LRRC8A-E). VRACs mediate regulatory volume decrease by releasing Cl- and organic osmolytes, including taurine. In the brain, taurine functions as both an osmolyte and an inhibitory neuromodulator, acting as an agonist at glycine and GABAA receptors. Here, we used RNAi and genetically modified mice to (i) determine the contribution of LRRC8 subunits to swelling-activated taurine release, and (ii) test whether brain VRACs contribute to systemic osmoregulation. In astrocyte cultures lacking the essential VRAC subunit LRRC8A, swelling-activated [3H]taurine release was reduced by ~90%. Similarly, in vivo brain microdialysis revealed a [≥]90% reduction in swelling-activated taurine release in brain-wide LRRC8A knockout mice (bLRRC8A KO). RNAi experiments further confirmed LRRC8D as a key determinant of VRAC-mediated taurine release, with Lrrc8d knockdown reducing swelling activated [3H]taurine efflux by >50%. RNA-seq revealed enrichment of Lrrc8d in the hypothalamus, where astrocytic taurine release is proposed to inhibit magnocellular neurons and suppress arginine vasopressin secretion during hypoosmotic conditions. We therefore tested whether disrupting brain VRACs impairs recovery from systemic hypoosmotic stress. bLRRC8A KO mice and mice with gene trap-mediated LRRC8D depletion were challenged with an intraperitoneal injection of sterile water (7.5% body weight, under anesthesia), and serum osmolality was monitored over time. Unexpectedly, neither model showed impaired recovery from hypoosmotic challenge. Overall, this study identifies LRRC8A/D-containing VRACs as the primary conduit for swelling-activated taurine release in the brain, yet indicates that this pathway is not essential for maintaining systemic fluid-electrolyte homeostasis.

articles.title: Slow Ionic Dynamics Reshape Bistability in a Biophysical Mean-Field Model of Brain Activity
articles.content: Brain states such as sleep, seizures, and resting wakefulness are often described in terms of transitions between distinct population states. Biophysically inspired mean-field models that couple neuronal firing statistics to slow ionic homeostasis provide a mechanistic bridge between detailed single-neuron physiology and macroscopic brain activity. Here we examine this issue in a biophysical mean-field model of cortical populations driven by potassium exchange and compare its dynamical repertoire with a matched spiking network across six physiological and pathological regimes. The fast subsystem contains a substantial region in which low- and high-activity fixed points coexist, but this conditional bistability is not inherited by the physiological resting branch of the complete slow-fast system. A generic fast-slow calculation identifies how feedback through a dynamical ionic variable changes the stability conditions of the fast subsystem, and an exact equilibrium reduction of the KIonEx-MF equations yields a single equilibrium on the physiological resting branch over the range examined. This resting state is excitable: perturbations generate intermittent synchronized events in both the mean-field and spiking-network descriptions. The results show how slow ionic dynamics can reshape conclusions drawn from a frozen fast subsystem and provide noise-driven excitability as an alternative route to spontaneous population transitions.

articles.title: Splanchnic-spinal transmission of gut-initiated α-synucleinopathy
articles.content: Gut-initiated -synucleinopathy is proposed to spread from the gastrointestinal tract to the CNS, contributing to Parkinson's disease (PD), but whether routes beyond the vagus nerve are involved remains unclear. Using complementary intracolonic rotenone and gastroduodenal -synuclein PFF models, we combined pathway-specific surgical interruption with longitudinal behavioral analysis and anatomical mapping of pathological -synuclein. In the intracolonic rotenone model, interruption of the prevertebral ganglia/splanchnic-spinal axis more strongly attenuated behavioral deficits and -synuclein pathology than vagotomy. In the gastroduodenal PFF model, both vagal and splanchnic-spinal pathways contributed to pathology propagation. Early after PFF inoculation, pathological -synuclein was detected in peripheral neural structures associated with both routes. Consistent with these findings, spinal pathology was evident in human PD. Together, these results identify the splanchnic-spinal pathway as a key component of body-first Parkinson's disease, broadening current models of peripheral-to-central disease progression and informing efforts to target early peripheral disease progression.

articles.title: Parvalbumin interneuron maturation reorganizes cortical population activity structure during development
articles.content: During brain development, spontaneous cortical activity undergoes a dramatic transformation from highly synchronous network events to less correlated and sparse neuronal firing that is thought to underlie more flexible neural coding. However, how the structure of population activity changes across this transition, what circuit mechanisms drive this reorganization, and the implications for information encoding have not been fully established. Using longitudinal in vivo calcium imaging in early postnatal mice, we demonstrate that cortical network desynchronization during the second postnatal week is accompanied by a redistribution of fractional variance from dominant, low-dimensional modes into many weaker dimensions, and a growing influence of GABAergic interneurons (INs) on the network. All-optical circuit interrogation revealed that parvalbumin (PV) INs, but not somatostatin (SST) INs, are sufficient to desynchronize the network and shift the distribution of population variance. Through targeted ablation of a fraction of PV INs, we show dimensionality is highly correlated with stimulus decoding accuracy. Furthermore, PV INs undergo a sharp increase in transcriptional maturation between postnatal day (P) 8 and 11, during which they preferentially enrich for synaptic genes. Lastly, a novel, biologically plausible, multi-cell-type computational model reproduced the developmental desynchronization and rise in dimensionality. Strikingly, without being constrained by perturbation data, the model accurately predicted the effects of each IN class on the network that we observed empirically.
articles.author: Wu, M. W., Mariani, M., Suresh, A., Kourdougli, N., Jiang, G., Kothari, A. J., Jain, T. S., Dipoppa, M., Portera-Cailliau, C.

articles.title: A coordinated and reproducible multicellular response to AD pathology
articles.content: While single-cell measurements of the Alzheimer's disease (AD) brain allow investigation of vulnerable cells in unprecedented depth, reported findings are heterogeneous, mostly descriptive and often ignore interdependence of cellular responses. Operationalization of these findings requires a multi-cellular model of AD that is robust and reproducible. Here, we utilize a coordinated multicellular community approach across 2.3 million nuclei from 427 ROSMAP donors to identify robust multicellular axes associated with AD pathology and sex. The AD signature comprised profound alteration to RORB-GABRG excitatory neurons and disrupted oligodendrocyte precursor cell signaling. A separate set of AD-related cell-type specific molecular processes with strong sexual dimorphism also emerged. Importantly, these signatures developed and ROSMAP predicted neuropathology and sex, respectively, in a completely independent dataset (SEA-AD). These findings altogether summarize a highly consistent multi-cellular response to AD pathology in the human brain, creating a baseline cellular model to which perturbation and treatment experiments can be compared.

SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1
articles.content:
Nature Neuroscience, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41593-026-02469-9

SIK3 kinase controls synaptic NMDA receptor recruitment by phosphorylating GluN1 at a single site. Loss or inhibition of SIK3 markedly reduces synaptic NMDARs, while a gain-of-function mutation increases GluN1 phosphorylation and NMDAR levels.

articles.title: A corticohypothalamic circuit that mediates maternal awakening to pup cries
articles.content:
Nature Neuroscience, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41593-026-02458-y

Tang, Wu et al. identify a brain circuit that enables mother mice to wake selectively to pup cries. Motherhood strengthens this pathway through increased dopamine receptor D1 expression, helping mothers to be responsive to offspring during sleep.

articles.title: Computational approaches to deep learning–driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review
articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.
